opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd place linear attention within a broader question the field keeps coming back to: how do we build sequence models that are both expressive and efficient?

Standard softmax attention is very powerful. Every token can look at every previous token directly, so in principle nothing is forgotten. But that comes at a cost. Compute grows quadratically with sequence length during training. At inference time you carry a KV cache that grows linearly with context. As we push toward very long contexts, long reasoning traces, and agentic settings where a model might run for thousands or millions of steps, that cost becomes a real bottleneck.

Linear attention, and the broader family it belongs to, which I'd loosely call linear RNNs or state-space-style models, takes the opposite tradeoff. You compress the whole history into a fixed-size state, often a matrix-valued memory. Each new token updates that state, and you read from it with the query. Inference then has constant memory and constant time per token, and training can still be parallelized with chunkwise algorithms that make good use of GPU tensor cores. That last part matters a lot. Early linear attention was elegant on paper but slow in practice. A lot of the recent progress has been about hardware-efficient implementations, so these models are actually competitive in wall-clock time.

The obvious weakness is that a fixed-size state has to forget something. So the research story of the last few years has been about making that memory smarter. One step was adding data-dependent gating and decay, as in models like GLA and Mamba, so the model can choose what to forget. Another was moving from a simple additive update to a delta-rule update, as in DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet. That update looks more like online learning: the model corrects its memory toward the right key-value association instead of just piling things on. This connects nicely to the "test-time training" view, where you can think of the recurrent state as a small model being trained on the context as you read it.

So in the broader landscape, I don't see linear attention as a replacement that will simply defeat transformers. I see it as one end of a design spectrum. Pure linear models still struggle on tasks that need precise retrieval over long contexts, things like exact recall. What's emerged in practice is hybrid architectures: mostly linear or gated-delta layers, with a few full-attention layers mixed in. That gets you most of the efficiency while keeping strong retrieval. Several industry models have moved in this direction, which tells me the idea has moved past being an academic curiosity.

More broadly, I think linear attention is a good lens for asking what "memory" in a neural network should look like. Softmax attention is a lossless but expensive memory. Linear RNNs are a compressed, learned memory. A lot of interesting future work, especially for long-horizon reasoning and agents, will come from figuring out how to combine the two well.

r002.rationale: It contrasts softmax attention’s quadratic training compute with linear attention’s fixed-size state and constant-time-per-token inference, describing linear attention as an efficient alternative.

fable-5.1.text:
Songlin Yang: I'd say linear attention is one answer to a very old question that keeps coming back in different clothes: how do you build a sequence model whose cost doesn't blow up with context length. Softmax attention is beautiful because it's exact, it's parallel, and it scales wonderfully with compute, but it carries a KV cache that grows linearly with the sequence, and the attention itself is quadratic. For a long time people treated that as the price of admission. Linear attention is the family of methods that says: keep the general shape of attention, keep the parallel training, but replace the ever-growing cache with a fixed-size state.

The way I think about it, there are really three lineages converging. One is the linear attention line, going back to Katharopoulos and the early kernelized-attention work, which asked whether you could drop the softmax and get a recurrent form. The second is the state-space line, S4, Mamba, which came from signal processing and control and arrived at structured recurrences from the other direction. The third is the older RNN tradition, fast weights, Hebbian updates, Schmidhuber's work in the nineties, which in hindsight was already describing an associative memory being written to and read from. Around 2023 and 2024 these all collapsed into basically one object: a linear recurrence with a matrix-valued state, where the design question is how you gate it, how you decay it, and how you update it. Gated linear attention, DeltaNet, Mamba2, RWKV, they're all points in that one space.

So where it sits in the broader LLM landscape: I don't think of it as a replacement for transformers so much as a component. The honest empirical picture is that pure linear models are competitive at moderate scale and on many benchmarks, but they still lose on tasks that need precise retrieval over long contexts, because a fixed-size state has to compress and softmax doesn't. The pragmatic thing, and what you see in production now, is hybrids: mostly linear layers with a few softmax layers sprinkled in. That gets you most of the inference efficiency while keeping the exact recall where it matters.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that this is as much a hardware story as a modeling story. The reason linear attention went from an academic curiosity to something people actually train at scale is that we figured out how to write it in a chunkwise form that maps onto tensor cores. Flash attention taught everyone that the algorithm that wins is the one that's friendly to the GPU, and linear attention had to learn that lesson too. A lot of my own work has been less about inventing a new recurrence and more about making the recurrences we already have run fast.

So if I had to summarize: it's the efficiency-and-memory axis of the field, it's where the RNN and SSM and attention communities finally met, and the interesting open questions now are about what the state should remember, how to update it in a more expressive way than a simple decay, and how far you can push the ratio of linear to softmax layers before you give something up.

astra-6.text:
I’d place linear attention within the broader effort to make language models more efficient, especially as context lengths grow. Standard attention is very flexible: each token can directly attend to earlier tokens. But the computation becomes expensive as the sequence gets longer, and during generation you have to maintain a growing key-value cache.

Linear attention changes that computation so you can summarize the past in a recurrent state. That gives you attractive efficiency properties, but it also creates the central research question: what information can that state retain, and how precisely can the model retrieve it later?

So I think it’s more than just a faster implementation of attention. It’s an exploration of a different way to represent and access memory. In the broader landscape, it sits alongside work on efficient attention, recurrent models, and state-space models. The important question is whether those architectural choices give us a better balance of model quality, training cost, and inference efficiency. Hybrid architectures are interesting in that respect, because different layers don’t necessarily need to handle memory in the same way.

sol-6.1.text:
I see linear attention as one part of the broader effort to make language models more efficient, especially as we ask them to process longer contexts. A lot of progress in language modeling has come from scaling, but scaling also makes the cost of the underlying architecture increasingly important.

Standard attention lets each token directly access earlier tokens, which is very powerful, but the cost grows with the sequence length. Linear attention changes that computation, often by summarizing the history in a fixed-size state. That gives it a close connection to recurrent models: you gain efficiency, but you have to think carefully about what information that state can retain and retrieve.

So I wouldn’t frame the research as simply replacing softmax attention with something cheaper. The interesting question is how to get a better tradeoff between efficiency and capability. Can we preserve strong language modeling, retrieval, and in-context learning while reducing the cost of long sequences? And where might hybrid architectures make sense? To me, linear attention is a way to explore those questions about memory and computation in language models.
